title: Lamrim: death
hook: death is certain, its time uncertain, only practice helps at that time

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first stair of the lamrim: this precious life, rare as a blind turtle finding the yoke. Today, the next stair.

A village asleep in a river valley. Lamps out, doors shut, everyone dreaming about tomorrow's chores. In the night the river rises, and by morning the village is gone. The Dhammapada uses that picture for a person wrapped up in family and possessions, carried off by death before they've looked up. It's not a gentle image, and it isn't meant to be. Yesterday the lamrim said this life is precious. Today it adds the other half, the one that gives the first its weight: this precious life will end, and nobody knows when.
screen: `A VILLAGE ASLEEP.` → `THE RIVER RISES IN THE NIGHT.` → `PRECIOUS, AND IT ENDS.`

segments.voice: You met this on day six hundred three, in the dart of grief; here the lamrim makes it a stair. First, death is certain. The lamrim doesn't ask anyone to dwell on gloom, only to notice that no one who was born has stayed. The great teachers died. The Buddha died. Every person in an old photograph is gone or going. None of this is news, yet the mind lives as if it were someone else's news. Second, the time is uncertain. A life has no fixed length. Healthy people die suddenly, the old sometimes outlive the young, and the things that keep a body alive, food, a car, a doctor's medicine, can in a bad moment be the things that end it. Tomorrow is not a promise; it's a likely guess. Third, at that time only practice helps. The Dhammapada says that when death seizes someone, sons are no help, nor a father, nor relatives. The lamrim adds wealth and the body itself. What goes with you, in this teaching, is the shape your mind has taken: the patience, the kindness, the clarity you actually practiced. Fourth, why it belongs here. Precious life alone can turn into a reason to relax. Precious life plus an unknown end turns into urgency, the good kind: not panic, but a clear sense of what matters today. And if thoughts of death feel close or heavy today, you don't have to carry them alone: in the US, call or text 988, or call local emergency help.
screen: `DEATH IS CERTAIN.` · `ITS TIME IS UNCERTAIN.` · `AT THAT TIME, ONLY PRACTICE HELPS.` · `PRECIOUS PLUS UNKNOWN: GOOD URGENCY.` · then, large: `CERTAIN, UNCERTAIN.`

segments.voice: Say quietly to yourself, this life will end, and let it sit for a few breaths; then, I don't know when. Ask gently, without pressure: if that's true, what matters today? If this feels too heavy right now, simply rest with the breath instead.
Lamrim, the next stair: death. Certain that it comes, uncertain when, and at that time only practice helps. Today's word.
Your line: certain, uncertain. Held together, they sort the important from the merely loud. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In lamrim practice, students meditate on death's certainty, the uncertainty of its time, and that only practice helps at death, reflecting on each point in turn during regular meditation sessions.

chat.says: Isn't thinking about death just depressing? Why would Buddhists do it on purpose?
options: It's meant to bring clarity, not gloom: life ends, the time is unknown, so what matters today?
It's meant to make you anxious, so you'll be too afraid to waste any time at all.
It's meant to show that life doesn't matter, since everything ends anyway.
chat.meaning: The lamrim pairs certain death with an uncertain time to bring good urgency, not panic: a clear sense of what matters today.
